claim: Auditory sensory outer hair cells are thought to amplify sound-induced basilar membrane vibration through a feedback mechanism to enhance hearing sensitivity.
source: Auditory sensory outer hair cells are thought to amplify sound-induced basilar membrane vibration through a feedback mechanism to enhance hearing sensitivity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific theory in the field, representing current understanding.

claim: For optimal amplification, the outer hair cell-generated force must act on the basilar membrane at an appropriate time at every cycle.
source: For optimal amplification, the outer hair cell-generated force must act on the basilar membrane at an appropriate time at every cycle.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement based on established understanding of cochlear mechanics.

claim: The temporal relationship between the outer hair cell-driven reticular lamina vibration and the basilar membrane vibration remains unclear.
source: However, the temporal relationship between the outer hair cell-driven reticular lamina vibration and the basilar membrane vibration remains unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: In living gerbil cochleae, the reticular lamina vibration occurs after, not before, the basilar membrane vibration.
source: By measuring sub-nanometer vibrations directly from outer hair cells using a custom-built heterodyne low-coherence interferometer, we demonstrate in living gerbil cochleae that the reticular lamina vibration occurs after, not before, the basilar membrane vibration.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental measurements using heterodyne low-coherence interferometry.

claim: The reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibrate in opposite directions at the cochlear base.
source: Both tone- and click-induced responses indicate that the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibrate in opposite directions at the cochlear base and they oscillate in phase near the best-frequency location.
evidence: This finding is supported by both tone and click response measurements presented in the study.

claim: The reticular lamina and basilar membrane oscillate in phase near the best-frequency location.
source: Both tone- and click-induced responses indicate that the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibrate in opposite directions at the cochlear base and they oscillate in phase near the best-frequency location.
evidence: This finding is supported by both tone and click response measurements presented in the study.

claim: Outer hair cells enhance hearing sensitivity through a global hydromechanical mechanism, rather than through a local mechanical feedback.
source: Our results suggest that outer hair cells enhance hearing sensitivity through a global hydromechanical mechanism, rather than through a local mechanical feedback as commonly supposed.
evidence: This is the main interpretation of the experimental findings, representing a new hypothesis based on the data.

claim: The exceptional sensitivity of mammalian hearing has been attributed to a micromechanical feedback system inside the cochlea, also called 'the cochlear amplifier' or 'cochlear active process'.
source: The exceptional sensitivity of mammalian hearing has been attributed to a micromechanical feedback system inside the cochlea, also called 'the cochlear amplifier' or 'cochlear active process' (Dallos et al., 2008; Davis, 1983; Fettiplace and Hackney, 2006; Hudspeth, 2014; Robles and Ruggero, 2001; Russell et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established literature in the field.

claim: When sound-induced basilar membrane vibrations deflect hair bundles of the outer hair cells, mechanoelectrical transduction of these cells generates the receptor potential.
source: When sound-induced basilar membrane vibrations deflect hair bundles of the outer hair cells, mechanoelectrical transduction of these cells generates the receptor potential (Dallos et al., 1982; Russell and Sellick, 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mammalian outer hair cells change their length and generate force primarily through somatic motility driven by the motor protein, prestin.
source: In response to the membrane potential change, mammalian outer hair cells change their length and generate force primarily through the somatic motility driven by the motor protein, prestin (Ashmore, 2008; Brownell et al., 1985; Liberman et al., 2002; Mammano and Ashmore, 1993; Mellado Lagarde et al., 2008; Ren et al., 2016a; Santos-Sacchi, 1989; Zheng et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The cellular force from outer hair cells is thought to be directly applied to the basilar membrane at its generation location on a cycle-by-cycle basis, consequently amplifying the sound-induced basilar membrane vibration and boosting hearing sensitivity.
source: This cellular force is thought to be directly applied to the basilar membrane at its generation location on a cycle-by-cycle basis, consequently amplifying the sound-induced basilar membrane vibration and boosting hearing sensitivity (Dallos et al., 2008; de Boer, 1995b; Dong and Olson, 2013; Hudspeth, 2014; Liu and Neely, 2009; Reichenbach and Hudspeth, 2014).
evidence: This represents the prevailing theory in the field, supported by citations.

claim: For optimal amplification, the cellular force must act on the basilar membrane at an appropriate time at every vibration cycle.
source: For optimal amplification, the cellular force must act on the basilar membrane at an appropriate time at every vibration cycle (Dallos et al., 2008; Nilsen and Russell, 1999).
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Timing of the cochlear feedback has been a central research topic in the field of auditory neuroscience since the cochlear amplifier was proposed.
source: Therefore, timing of the cochlear feedback has been a central research topic in the field of auditory neuroscience since the cochlear amplifier was proposed (Ashmore, 2008; Davis, 1983; Gold, 1948; Gummer et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement about the research field is supported by citations to historical and contemporary literature.

claim: Cochlear amplification depends on normal cochlear metabolism and the integrity of cochlear mechanical properties.
source: Because cochlear amplification depends on normal cochlear metabolism and the integrity of cochlear mechanical properties (Cooper and Rhode, 1992; Fisher et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Nuttall et al., 1991; Ren and Nuttall, 2001; Rhode, 1971; Robles and Ruggero, 2001; Ruggero and Rich, 1991; van der Heijden and Versteegh, 2015), the cochlear feedback has to be investigated ultimately in living cochleae.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The cochlear feedback has to be investigated ultimately in living cochleae.
source: Because cochlear amplification depends on normal cochlear metabolism and the integrity of cochlear mechanical properties (Cooper and Rhode, 1992; Fisher et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Nuttall et al., 1991; Ren and Nuttall, 2001; Rhode, 1971; Robles and Ruggero, 2001; Ruggero and Rich, 1991; van der Heijden and Versteegh, 2015), the cochlear feedback has to be investigated ultimately in living cochleae.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the dependence of cochlear amplification on living conditions.

claim: Timing of cochlear feedback was studied in vivo by measuring basilar membrane vibrations at different locations across the width of the basilar membrane in guinea pig.
source: Timing of cochlear feedback was studied in vivo by measuring basilar membrane vibrations at different locations across the width of the basilar membrane in guinea pig (Nilsen and Russell, 1999).
evidence: This describes a prior study, supported by citation.

claim: Forces generated by the outer hair cells directly drive the region of the basilar membrane beneath the Deiters' cells.
source: Based on their observation, the authors suggest that forces generated by the outer hair cells directly drive the region of the basilar membrane beneath the Deiters' cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from a prior study (Nilsen and Russell, 1999), referenced in the text.

claim: The phase of the reticular lamina vibration led the phase of the basilar membrane vibration at the best frequency in guinea pigs.
source: The temporal relationship between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration was previously observed in guinea pigs using a time-domain optical coherence tomography system as a homodyne interferometer (Chen et al., 2011). It was reported that the phase of the reticular lamina vibration led the phase of the basilar membrane vibration at the best frequency (Figure 5, Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes findings from a prior study, supported by citation.

claim: The phase lead of reticular lamina over basilar membrane has been thought to ensure the right timing of the outer hair cell force for cochlear amplification.
source: This phase lead has been thought to ensure the right timing of the outer hair cell force for cochlear amplification.
evidence: This represents a prevailing interpretation in the field based on prior observations.

claim: Mouse micromechanical data measured using a heterodyne low-coherence interferometer showed no significant phase difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration at the best frequency.
source: However, the mouse micromechanical data measured using a heterodyne low-coherence interferometer showed no significant phase difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration at the best frequency (Ren et al., 2016b).
evidence: This describes findings from a prior study by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: The discrepancy between guinea pig and mouse data may have been caused by the animal species and technical differences (mouse versus guinea pig and homodyne interferometry versus heterodyne interferometry).
source: This discrepancy may have been caused by the animal species and technical differences, that is mouse versus guinea pig and homodyne interferometry versus heterodyne interferometry.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of discrepancies between studies.

claim: The timing of the cochlear feedback remains unclear despite recent studies measuring micromechanical responses in living cochleae.
source: Although a number of studies have been conducted recently to measure micromechanical responses in living cochleae (Gao et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2016; Ramamoorthy et al., 2016; Recio-Spinoso and Oghalai, 2017; Cooper et al., 2018) the timing of the cochlear feedback remains unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge despite recent research efforts, supported by citations.

claim: The apical end of outer hair cells is directly connected to the reticular lamina.
source: Since the apical end of outer hair cells is directly connected to the reticular lamina, the reticular lamina vibration can reflect the movement of the outer hair cell under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about cochlear structure.

claim: The reticular lamina vibration can reflect the movement of the outer hair cell under physiological conditions.
source: Since the apical end of outer hair cells is directly connected to the reticular lamina, the reticular lamina vibration can reflect the movement of the outer hair cell under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical connection between outer hair cells and reticular lamina.

claim: The timing of the cochlear feedback was determined by measuring the latency difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration using a custom-built heterodyne low-coherence interferometer.
source: Therefore, the timing of the cochlear feedback was determined in this study by measuring the latency difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration using a custom-built heterodyne low-coherence interferometer (Hong and Freeman, 2006; Ren et al., 2016a; Ren et al., 2016b).
evidence: This describes the methodology of the current study, with citations to the technique.

claim: The gerbil is one of the most commonly used animals for auditory research.
source: The present data collected from the gerbil, one of the most commonly used animals for auditory research, demonstrate for the first time that the reticular lamina vibrates after, not before, the basilar membrane vibration.
evidence: This is general knowledge about animal models in auditory research.

claim: This is the first demonstration that the reticular lamina vibrates after, not before, the basilar membrane vibration.
source: The present data collected from the gerbil, one of the most commonly used animals for auditory research, demonstrate for the first time that the reticular lamina vibrates after, not before, the basilar membrane vibration.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: The displacement of the reticular lamina response to 30 dB SPL tones increased and then decreased with frequency, forming a sharp peak at ~26 kHz (best frequency).
source: The displacement of the reticular lamina response to 30 dB SPL tones (0 dB SPL = 20 µPa) increased and then decreased with frequency, forming a sharp peak at ~26 kHz (best frequency, BF) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Displacements of the reticular lamina increased proportionally with sound level at frequencies < 15 kHz.
source: While displacements increased proportionally with sound level at frequencies < 15 kHz, they increased at a much smaller rate near the best frequency.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data describing the frequency-dependent response.

claim: Reticular lamina displacements increased at a much smaller rate near the best frequency with increasing sound level.
source: While displacements increased proportionally with sound level at frequencies < 15 kHz, they increased at a much smaller rate near the best frequency.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data indicating nonlinear compression.

claim: The response peak of the reticular lamina became broader and shifted toward low frequencies as the sound level increased.
source: The response peak became broader and shifted toward low frequencies as the sound level increased.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At 80 dB SPL, the reticular lamina displacement curve showed no response peak.
source: In contrast to sharp tuning at 30 dB SPL, the displacement curve at 80 dB SPL showed no response peak.
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Displacements of the basilar membrane at 30 and 40 dB SPL were ~10 fold smaller than those of the reticular lamina not only near the best frequency but also at lower frequencies.
source: Displacements of the basilar membrane at 30 and 40 dB SPL were ~10 fold smaller than those of the reticular lamina not only near the best frequency but also at lower frequencies (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Basilar membrane response reached the maximum at ~26 kHz as did the reticular lamina.
source: Basilar membrane response also reached the maximum at ~26 kHz as did the reticular lamina.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data showing similar best frequencies.

claim: For ~333 fold sound level increase from 30 to 80 dB SPL, the displacement of the basilar membrane at ~26 kHz increased by ~23 fold compared with only ~3.3 fold increase of the reticular lamina displacement at the same frequency.
source: For ~333 fold sound level increase from 30 to 80 dB SPL, the displacement of the basilar membrane at ~26 kHz increased by ~23 fold compared with only ~3.3 fold increase of the reticular lamina displacement at the same frequency.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the experimental data showing differential compression.

claim: The reticular lamina showed ~40 dB nonlinear compression near the best frequency.
source: The reticular lamina showed ~40 dB nonlinear compression near the best frequency, which is ~17 dB greater than that of the basilar membrane (~23 dB).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The basilar membrane showed ~23 dB nonlinear compression near the best frequency.
source: The reticular lamina showed ~40 dB nonlinear compression near the best frequency, which is ~17 dB greater than that of the basilar membrane (~23 dB).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Phase responses of the reticular lamina are similar to those of the basilar membrane except for a slightly steeper phase slope at frequencies < 15 kHz.
source: Phase responses of the reticular lamina (Figure 1E) are similar to those of the basilar membrane (Figure 1F) except for a slightly steeper phase slope at frequencies < 15 kHz.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: Highly sensitive, sharply tuned nonlinear responses of the reticular lamina and basilar membrane in the gerbil are similar to those measured from the basal turn of mouse cochleae under sensitive conditions.
source: Thus, highly sensitive, sharply tuned nonlinear responses of the reticular lamina and basilar membrane in the gerbil (Figure 1A–D) are similar to those measured from the basal turn of mouse cochleae under sensitive conditions (Ren et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a comparison between current data and previously published data, supported by citation.

claim: All displacement ratios of reticular lamina to basilar membrane are greater than one, indicating that reticular lamina vibrations were greater than those of the basilar membrane at different frequencies and sound levels.
source: All displacement ratios are greater than one, indicating that reticular lamina vibrations were greater than those of the basilar membrane at different frequencies and sound levels.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Near the best frequency (~26 kHz), the displacement ratio of reticular lamina to basilar membrane was ~10 at 30 dB SPL, decreasing with sound level and becoming ~1.5 at 80 dB SPL.
source: Near the best frequency (~26 kHz), the displacement ratio was ~10 at 30 dB SPL, decreasing with sound level and becoming ~1.5 at 80 dB SPL.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The greatest displacement ratios of reticular lamina to basilar membrane were observed at frequencies far below the best frequency and at high sound levels.
source: In contrast to well documented sharply tuned basilar membrane vibration at the best frequency (Robles and Ruggero, 2001), the greatest displacement ratios were observed at frequencies far below the best frequency and at high sound levels.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data that contrasts with established knowledge.

claim: At frequencies < 10 kHz, reticular lamina phase led basilar membrane phase by up to 180 degrees.
source: At frequencies < 10 kHz, reticular lamina phase led basilar membrane phase by up to 180 degrees.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The phase lead of reticular lamina over basilar membrane decreased with frequency and the phase difference became slightly negative at the best frequency.
source: This phase lead decreased with frequency and the phase difference became slightly negative at the best frequency.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The slope of the linear regression line of the phase difference curve at 70 dB SPL indicates that the latency of the reticular lamina is ~20 µs greater than that of the basilar membrane.
source: The slope of the linear regression line (thick black dotted) of the phase difference curve at 70 dB SPL indicates that the latency of the reticular lamina is ~20 µs greater than that of the basilar membrane.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Displacements of the reticular lamina vibration decreased dramatically at all frequencies under postmortem conditions.
source: Compared to sensitive responses (red lines in Figure 2A), displacements of the reticular lamina vibration decreased dramatically at all frequencies under postmortem conditions (blue lines in Figure 2A), while the basilar membrane vibration decreased only near the best frequency (blues lines in Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data comparing sensitive and postmortem conditions shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The basilar membrane vibration decreased only near the best frequency under postmortem conditions.
source: Compared to sensitive responses (red lines in Figure 2A), displacements of the reticular lamina vibration decreased dramatically at all frequencies under postmortem conditions (blue lines in Figure 2A), while the basilar membrane vibration decreased only near the best frequency (blues lines in Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data comparing sensitive and postmortem conditions shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The broad peaks of reticular lamina and basilar membrane postmortem responses shifted toward low frequencies compared to the sharp peak of 30 dB SPL sensitive responses at ~26 kHz.
source: In contrast to the sharp peak of 30 dB SPL sensitive responses at ~26 kHz, the broad peaks of reticular lamina and basilar membrane postmortem responses shifted toward low frequencies (blue lines in Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data comparing sensitive and postmortem responses.

claim: The reticular lamina vibration decreased by >10 fold at frequencies < 20 kHz under postmortem conditions, although the basilar membrane vibration did not decrease significantly at the same frequencies.
source: Although the basilar membrane vibration at frequencies < 20 kHz did not decrease significantly, the reticular lamina vibration decreased by >10 fold over the same frequency range.

claim: The observation that reticular lamina vibration decreased at low frequencies under postmortem conditions is unexpected since cochlear amplification has been believed to be effective only near the best frequency.
source: This is unexpected since cochlear amplification has been believed to be effective only near the best frequency (Robles and Ruggero, 2001).

claim: Postmortem responses showed linear growth, indicated by overlapping curves at different sound levels.
source: The overlapping blue curves in Figure 2C,D and the equally separated blue curves in Figure 2A,B indicate linear growth for postmortem responses.

claim: The reticular lamina phase decreased by up to 180 degrees at frequencies < 10 kHz under postmortem conditions.
source: In contrast to the lack of significant change in basilar membrane phase (Figure 2F), the reticular lamina phase decreased by up to 180 degrees at frequencies < 10 kHz (Figure 2E).

claim: There was no significant change in basilar membrane phase under postmortem conditions.
source: In contrast to the lack of significant change in basilar membrane phase (Figure 2F), the reticular lamina phase decreased by up to 180 degrees at frequencies < 10 kHz (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data comparing sensitive and postmortem conditions shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The displacement ratio of the reticular lamina to basilar membrane vibration decreased dramatically at all frequencies under postmortem conditions.
source: The displacement ratio of the reticular lamina to basilar membrane vibration decreased dramatically at all frequencies (compare blue to red lines in Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data comparing sensitive and postmortem conditions shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The frequency-dependent phase lead of reticular lamina over basilar membrane was absent under postmortem conditions.
source: The frequency-dependent phase lead (red lines in Figure 2H) was absent under postmortem conditions (blue lines in Figure 2H).

source: Although the measurements were taken from similar longitudinal locations in the basal turn of the cochlea in both species, the best frequencies of the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration in the gerbil are significantly lower than those in the mouse.
evidence: This is a comparison between current gerbil data and previously published mouse data.

claim: In postmortem gerbil cochleae, the basilar membrane vibrated more than the reticular lamina.

claim: The displacement ratio of the reticular lamina vibration to the basilar membrane vibration was the largest at the low-frequency end and decreased with frequency reaching the lowest level near the best frequency.

claim: The averaged phase data show that the reticular lamina phase led the basilar membrane phase by >135 degrees at low frequencies.
source: The averaged phase data show that the reticular lamina phase led the basilar membrane phase by >135 degrees at low frequencies.

source: This phase lead decreased with frequency and approached zero near the best frequency (Figure 3B,D,F,H).

claim: The magnitude ratio of reticular lamina to basilar membrane decreased with the sound level near the best frequency.

claim: The phase difference between reticular lamina and basilar membrane showed no significant change with sound level near the best frequency.
source: While the magnitude ratio decreased with the sound level near the best frequency (Figure 3I), the phase difference showed no significant change at the same frequency (Figure 3J).

claim: The latency differences derived from the slope of the phase difference curves show no significant change across stimulus levels (ANOVA test: F = 0.037, p=0.990).
source: Consequently, the latency differences derived from the slope of the phase difference curves show no significant change across stimulus levels (ANOVA test: F = 0.037, p=0.990).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The grouped data from seven gerbils at four different sound levels demonstrate that the latency of the reticular lamina vibration is ~17.9 µs greater than that of the basilar membrane (17.9 ± 0.6 µs, n = 28).
source: The grouped data from seven gerbils at four different sound levels demonstrate that the latency of the reticular lamina vibration is ~17.9 µs greater than that of the basilar membrane (17.9 ± 0.6 µs, n = 28) (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The latency difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration in mice (12.1 ± 0.6 µs, n = 5) is significantly smaller than that in gerbils (17.9 ± 0.6 µs, n = 28) (t = 7.775, p<0.01, n = 33).
source: The latency difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration in mice (12.1 ± 0.6 µs, n = 5) is significantly smaller than that in gerbils (17.9 ± 0.6 µs, n = 28) (t = 7.775, p<0.01, n = 33).

claim: The smaller latency difference in mice likely results from higher best frequencies.
source: The smaller latency difference in mice likely results from higher best frequencies.

claim: The basilar membrane moved toward the scala vestibuli in response to a 10-µs rarefaction click, indicated by the first positive peak.

claim: The peak magnitude of the reticular lamina displacement is ~eight fold larger than that of the basilar membrane vibration in response to clicks.

claim: The peak magnitude of the basilar membrane vibration increased proportionally with the sound level in response to clicks.

source: These changes indicate that the reticular lamina moves passively following the basilar membrane vibration under postmortem conditions.

claim: The time-domain data confirm that the reticular lamina vibrates after, not before, the basilar membrane vibration.
source: Thus, the time-domain data in Figure 4 confirm that the reticular lamina vibrates after, not before, the basilar membrane vibration.

claim: The initially opposite displacements and following synchronous movements of the reticular lamina and the basilar membrane are consistent with the ~180° phase difference at low frequencies and in-phase vibrations at the best frequency.
source: Moreover, the initially opposite displacements and following synchronous movements of the reticular lamina and the basilar membrane in Figure 4A and C are consistent with the ~180° phase difference at low frequencies and in-phase vibrations at the best frequency in Figure 3.
evidence: This is an inference connecting observations from click responses to tone responses.

claim: The latency of the reticular lamina vibration is greater than that of the basilar membrane vibration.
source: This paper reports the first in vivo measurement of the latency difference between the outer hair cell-driven reticular lamina vibration and the basilar membrane vibration. The present data demonstrate that the latency of the reticular lamina vibration is greater than that of the basilar membrane vibration, and there is no significant phase difference between the two structures near the best frequencies.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental measurements.

claim: There is no significant phase difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane near the best frequencies.
source: This paper reports the first in vivo measurement of the latency difference between the outer hair cell-driven reticular lamina vibration and the basilar membrane vibration. The present data demonstrate that the latency of the reticular lamina vibration is greater than that of the basilar membrane vibration, and there is no significant phase difference between the two structures near the best frequencies.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The current result is consistent with the mouse data measured using heterodyne interferometry.
source: This result is consistent with the mouse data measured using heterodyne interferometry (Ren et al., 2016b) but inconsistent with the guinea pig data, which showed that the phase of the reticular lamina vibration leads the phase of the basilar membrane vibration by ~90° at the best frequency and the phase lead decreases with sound pressure level (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison between current findings and previously published data, supported by citations.

claim: The current result is inconsistent with the guinea pig data, which showed that the phase of the reticular lamina vibration leads the phase of the basilar membrane vibration by ~90° at the best frequency and the phase lead decreases with sound pressure level.
source: This result is consistent with the mouse data measured using heterodyne interferometry (Ren et al., 2016b) but inconsistent with the guinea pig data, which showed that the phase of the reticular lamina vibration leads the phase of the basilar membrane vibration by ~90° at the best frequency and the phase lead decreases with sound pressure level (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison between current findings and previously published data, supported by citation.

claim: The current result confirms recent studies in the mouse and in the guinea pig that the physiologically vulnerable reticular lamina vibration is significantly greater than the basilar membrane vibration not only at the best frequency but also at low frequencies.
source: The current result also confirms recent studies in the mouse (Ren et al., 2016b) and in the guinea pig (Recio-Spinoso and Oghalai, 2017) that the physiologically vulnerable reticular lamina vibration is significantly greater than the basilar membrane vibration not only at the best frequency but also at low frequencies.
evidence: This is a comparison between current findings and previously published data, supported by citations.

claim: An ~90° phase lead of the reticular lamina vibration is thought to be required for cochlear feedback to amplify basilar membrane vibration.
source: Since an ~90° phase lead of the reticular lamina vibration is thought to be required for cochlear feedback to amplify basilar membrane vibration (Chen et al., 2011; Gummer et al., 1996; Nilsen and Russell, 1999; Robles and Ruggero, 2001; Russell and Nilsen, 1997), and since cochlear amplification has been predicted to work only near the best frequency location (de Boer, 1995a; Dong and Olson, 2013; Liu et al., 2017; Liu and Neely, 2009; Meaud and Grosh, 2012; Motallebzadeh et al., 2018; Ni et al., 2016132016; Ramamoorthy et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2016), the current result is inconsistent with the local cochlear feedback hypothesis.
evidence: This is a statement of prevailing theory, supported by citations.

claim: Cochlear amplification has been predicted to work only near the best frequency location.
source: Since an ~90° phase lead of the reticular lamina vibration is thought to be required for cochlear feedback to amplify basilar membrane vibration (Chen et al., 2011; Gummer et al., 1996; Nilsen and Russell, 1999; Robles and Ruggero, 2001; Russell and Nilsen, 1997), and since cochlear amplification has been predicted to work only near the best frequency location (de Boer, 1995a; Dong and Olson, 2013; Liu et al., 2017; Liu and Neely, 2009; Meaud and Grosh, 2012; Motallebzadeh et al., 2018; Ni et al., 2016132016; Ramamoorthy et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2016), the current result is inconsistent with the local cochlear feedback hypothesis.
evidence: This is a statement of prevailing theory, supported by citations.

claim: The current result is inconsistent with the local cochlear feedback hypothesis.
source: Since an ~90° phase lead of the reticular lamina vibration is thought to be required for cochlear feedback to amplify basilar membrane vibration (Chen et al., 2011; Gummer et al., 1996; Nilsen and Russell, 1999; Robles and Ruggero, 2001; Russell and Nilsen, 1997), and since cochlear amplification has been predicted to work only near the best frequency location (de Boer, 1995a; Dong and Olson, 2013; Liu et al., 2017; Liu and Neely, 2009; Meaud and Grosh, 2012; Motallebzadeh et al., 2018; Ni et al., 2016132016; Ramamoorthy et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2016), the current result is inconsistent with the local cochlear feedback hypothesis.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings in relation to existing theory.

claim: The latency difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration supports the global hydromechanical mechanism for cochlear amplification.
source: Instead, the latency difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration found in this study supports the global hydromechanical mechanism for cochlear amplification (Ren et al., 2016b), which is discussed below.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: At 30 dB SPL, a tone-induced response occurred at a < 0.2 mm region at the best-frequency location.
source: While a 30 dB SPL tone-induced response occurred at a < 0.2 mm region at the best-frequency location (Figure 5A,C), a 70 dB SPL tone-induced vibration extended from the best-frequency location to the base (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: At 70 dB SPL, a tone-induced vibration extended from the best-frequency location to the base.
source: While a 30 dB SPL tone-induced response occurred at a < 0.2 mm region at the best-frequency location (Figure 5A,C), a 70 dB SPL tone-induced vibration extended from the best-frequency location to the base (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: The overlapping phase curves near the 2.05 mm location indicate that the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibrated approximately in the same direction at the best-frequency location.
source: The overlapping phase curves near the 2.05 mm location (blue and red lines in Figure 5C,D) indicate that the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibrated approximately in the same direction at the best-frequency location.
evidence: This is an inference from the phase data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The ~180 degree separation between phase curves near the cochlear base indicates opposite vibrations of the reticular lamina and basilar membrane.
source: The ~180 degree separation between the blue and red lines near the cochlear base (Figure 5D) indicates opposite vibrations of the reticular lamina and basilar membrane.
evidence: This is an inference from the phase data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At low sound levels, reticular lamina vibration is dominated by outer hair cell-driven movement.
source: The overlapping blue and green lines in Figure 5A and C indicate that, at low sound levels, reticular lamina vibration is dominated by outer hair cell-driven movement.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of measured and calculated responses shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: At 70 dB SPL, the outer hair cell-driven responses saturated near the best-frequency location.
source: At 70 dB SPL, the outer hair cell-driven responses saturated near the best-frequency location, indicated by the diverged blue and green lines near the response peak (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of measured and calculated responses shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When the basilar membrane moves upward to the scala vestibuli near the cochlear base, depolarized outer hair cells shorten and induce a large downward reticular lamina displacement.
source: When the basilar membrane moves upward to the scala vestibuli near the cochlear base (red arrow at 0.8 mm in Figure 5F), depolarized outer hair cells shorten and induce a large downward reticular lamina displacement (green arrow at 0.8 mm in Figure 5F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 5F, incorporating knowledge of outer hair cell physiology.

claim: The opposite movements of reticular lamina and basilar membrane create a positive fluid pressure between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane at the cochlear base.
source: While this movement creates a positive fluid pressure between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane at the cochlear base (0.7–1.2 mm in Figure 5F,G), the reticular lamina at locations ~ 1.2–1.8 mm, however, moves upward (green arrows near 1.6 mm in Figure 5F), resulting in a negative fluid pressure inside the cochlear partition.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed movements, applying principles of fluid mechanics.

claim: The reticular lamina at locations ~ 1.2–1.8 mm moves upward, resulting in a negative fluid pressure inside the cochlear partition.
source: While this movement creates a positive fluid pressure between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane at the cochlear base (0.7–1.2 mm in Figure 5F,G), the reticular lamina at locations ~ 1.2–1.8 mm, however, moves upward (green arrows near 1.6 mm in Figure 5F), resulting in a negative fluid pressure inside the cochlear partition.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed movements, applying principles of fluid mechanics.

claim: The pressure gradient from the base to an apical location likely results in fluid movement in the apical direction inside the cochlear partition.
source: This pressure gradient from the base to an apical location likely results in fluid movement in the apical direction inside the cochlear partition (blue arrows in Figure 5F,G) as demonstrated in vitro by electrically stimulating the organ of Corti (Karavitaki and Mountain, 2007; Zagadou and Mountain, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the pressure gradient, supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: The longitudinal fluid movement can travel forward to the best-frequency location as a result of the basilar membrane traveling wave.
source: Since the organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane, the longitudinal fluid movement can travel forward to the best-frequency location as a result of the basilar membrane traveling wave.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge and the traveling wave mechanism.

claim: A large population of outer hair cells from a broad cochlear area can change the fluid space between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane at the best frequency location on a cycle-by-cycle basis, consequently enhancing the reticular lamina vibration.
source: Thus, a large population of outer hair cells from a broad cochlear area can change the fluid space between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane at the best frequency location on a cycle-by-cycle basis, consequently enhancing the reticular lamina vibration.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental observations and inferences about fluid movement.

claim: In-phase vibrations of the reticular lamina and basilar membrane result in constructive interference near the best-frequency location, which further enhances reticular lamina vibration.
source: In addition, in-phase vibrations of the reticular lamina and basilar membrane result in constructive interference near the best-frequency location (Figure 5E,F,G), which further enhances reticular lamina vibration at the apical end of outer hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed in-phase relationship, applying principles of wave interference.

claim: The magnitude of the constructive interference decreases as phase differences move into destructive interference regimes at frequencies below and above the best frequency.
source: The magnitude of the resulting constructive interference decreases as phase differences move into destructive interference regimes at frequencies below and above the best frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on wave interference principles applied to the observed phase relationships.

claim: Frequency dependent interference may enhance the tuning of the reticular lamina vibration, but its effects are probably relatively small due to the large magnitude difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration.
source: While this frequency dependent interference may consequently enhance the tuning of the reticular lamina vibration, its effects probably is relatively small due to the large magnitude difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration.
evidence: This is a speculation about the relative importance of interference effects.

claim: The interaction between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane at low frequencies may be involved in two-tone suppression of the auditory nerve or basilar membrane response.
source: The interaction between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane at low frequencies may also be involved in two-tone suppression of the auditory nerve or basilar membrane response (Delgutte, 1990; Ruggero et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a speculation about a possible functional role, supported by citations to studies on two-tone suppression.

claim: The proposed global hydromechanical mechanism is consistent with the observation that auditory nerve activities can be suppressed by stimulating medial olivocochlear efferents or by a low-frequency bias tone not only at the best frequency but also at tail (low) frequencies.
source: It has been shown that the proposed global hydromechanical mechansm is consistent with the observation that auditory nerve activities can be suppressed by stimulating medial olivocochlear efferents or by a low-frequency bias tone not only at the best frequency but also at tail (low) frequencies (Nam and Guinan, 2017; Stankovic and Guinan, 1999).
evidence: This is a statement about consistency between the proposed mechanism and prior observations, supported by citations.

claim: The outer hair cell-driven reticular lamina vibration likely results in fluid movement in the subtectorial space and consequently stimulates inner hair cells.
source: Since the stereocilia bundles of both the inner and outer hair cells are anchored in the hair cell cuticular plates which make up a portion of the reticular lamina, the outer hair cell-driven reticular lamina vibration likely results in fluid movement in the subtectorial space and consequently stimulates inner hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge and the observed reticular lamina vibration.

claim: Electrical stimulation of outer hair cells of guinea pig cochleae resulted in a counterphasic motion of the tectorial membrane and inner hair cells at frequencies below 3 kHz in vitro.
source: It has been shown in vitro that electrical stimulation of outer hair cells of guinea pig cochleae resulted in a counterphasic motion of the tectorial membrane and inner hair cells at frequencies below 3 kHz (Nowotny and Gummer, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about prior in vitro findings, supported by citation.

claim: The counterphasic motion of the tectorial membrane and inner hair cells was believed to indicate direct fluid coupling between outer hair cells and inner hair cells through a pulsatile fluid motion.
source: This result was believed to indicate direct fluid coupling between outer hair cells and inner hair cells through a pulsatile fluid motion.
evidence: This is an interpretation from a prior study.

claim: Outer hair cell stereocilia not only move sideways but also change length in response to sound stimulation in vitro.
source: It has also been demonstrated in vitro that outer hair cell stereocilia not only move sideways but also change length in response to sound stimulation (Hakizimana et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about prior in vitro findings, supported by citation.

claim: Large bundle deflection was observed when the stereocilia length change was small, indicating that hair cells are maximally stimulated when the stereocilia length change is minimal.
source: The large bundle deflection was observed when the length change was small, indicating that hair cells are maximally stimulated when the stereocilia length change is minimal.
evidence: This is an interpretation from a prior study.

claim: The stereocilia length change suggests the interaction between the reticular lamina vibration and the tectorial membrane vibration.
source: Considering the firm connection of the tallest stereocilia to the tectorial membrane, the stereocilia length change also suggests the interaction between the reticular lamina vibration and the tectorial membrane vibration.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge and prior observations.

claim: Outer hair cells may play a role in the traveling wave on the tectorial membrane.
source: Thus, outer hair cells may also play a role in the traveling wave on the tectorial membrane, which has been demonstrated in vitro (Ghaffari et al., 2007; Ghaffari et al., 2010) and in vivo (Dong and Cooper, 2006; Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Recio-Spinoso and Oghalai, 2017; Rhode and Cooper, 1996).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating tectorial membrane traveling waves.

claim: The interaction between the reticular lamina and tectorial membrane vibration may enhance the stimulus to the inner hair cells and boost hearing sensitivity.
source: The interaction between the reticular lamina and tectorial membrane vibration may enhance the stimulus to the inner hair cells and boost hearing sensitivity.
evidence: This is a speculation about a possible mechanism for enhancing hearing sensitivity.

claim: Specific mechanisms on how the outer hair cell-driven reticular lamina vibration stimulates inner hair cells remain to be determined experimentally until in vivo micromechanical measurements with cellular spatial resolution become available.
source: Specific mechanisms on how the outer hair cell-driven reticular lamina vibration stimulates inner hair cells, however, remain to be determined experimentally until in vivo micromechanical measurements with cellular spatial resolution become available.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge and future research needs.

claim: The observed additional delay of the reticular lamina vibration was likely caused by mechanoelectrical and electromechanical transduction of outer hair cells and mechanical coupling inside the cochlear partition.
source: The observed additional delay of the reticular lamina vibration was likely caused by mechanoelectrical (Corey and Hudspeth, 1979) and electromechanical (Brownell et al., 1985) transduction of outer hair cells and mechanical coupling inside the cochlear partition.
evidence: This is a speculation about the causes of the observed delay, supported by citations to relevant processes.

claim: Delays for prestin-associated currents in vitro are longer than the latency difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration in vivo, but they vary with the membrane voltage of outer hair cells.
source: Although delays for prestin-associated currents in vitro (Santos-Sacchi and Tan, 2018) are longer than the latency difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration in vivo, they vary with the membrane voltage of outer hair cells.
evidence: This is a comparison between in vitro measurements and current in vivo findings, supported by citation.

claim: Voltage excitation away from the resting membrane potential has been shown to have a faster response in outer hair cells.
source: Voltage excitation away from the resting membrane potential has been shown to have a faster response.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge of outer hair cell physiology.

claim: The depolarized resting potential can minimize the outer hair cell time constant and expand the bandwidth of the membrane filter by activating voltage-dependent K+ conductance.
source: Moreover, the depolarized resting potential can minimize the outer hair cell time constant and expanding the bandwidth of the membrane filter by activating voltage-dependent K + conductance (Johnson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about outer hair cell physiology, supported by citation.

claim: Mechanical loads on the outer hair cells, such as in vivo condition, could further improve the cell's frequency response.
source: Mechanical loads on the outer hair cells, such as in vivo condition, could further improve the cell's frequency response (Iwasa, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about outer hair cell mechanics, supported by citation.

claim: The acoustical and cellular forces to and from the outer hair cells have to be transmitted through Deiters' cells, since Deiters' cells are located between the outer hair cells and the basilar membrane.
source: Since Deiters' cells are located between the outer hair cells and the basilar membrane, the acoustical and cellular forces to and from the outer hair cells have to be transmitted through Deiters' cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The soft Deiter's cell soma likely induces delays, which can contribute to the delay difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration.
source: The soft Deiter's cell soma likely induces delays, which can contribute to the delay difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration.
evidence: This is a speculation about a possible source of delay.

claim: If the connection between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane is rigid, the reticular lamina should move passively following the basilar membrane travelling wave with equal magnitude and phase when the outer hair cell-generated force is absent under postmortem conditions.
source: When the outer hair cell-generated force is absent under postmortem conditions, the reticular lamina should move passively following the basilar membrane travelling wave with equal magnitude and phase, if the connection between the two structures is rigid.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on mechanical principles.

claim: The larger postmortem magnitude and phase difference in gerbils than those in mice indicate that the mechanical coupling between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane in the gerbil may not be as tight as that in the mouse.
source: The larger postmortem magnitude and phase difference in gerbils (Figure 2) than those in mice (Figure 2G and H, Ren et al., 2016b) indicate that the mechanical coupling between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane in the gerbil may not be as tight as that in the mouse.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of postmortem data between species.

claim: A 17.9-µs latency difference is negligible compared to a large time period at a low frequency and results in an insignificant phase difference.
source: Compared to a large time period (T) at a low frequency (f) (T = 1/f) (such as T = 2,000 µs, where f = 500 Hz), a 17.9-µs latency difference (Figure 3J) is negligible and results in an insignificant phase difference.
evidence: This is a calculation demonstrating the relationship between latency and phase at low frequencies.

claim: The ~180 degree phase difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration at a low frequency mainly reflects the opposite movements of both ends of outer hair cells.
source: Thus, the ~180 degree phase difference between the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibration at a low frequency mainly reflects the opposite movements of both ends of outer hair cells (Brownell et al., 1985).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phase difference, supported by citation to in vitro observations.

claim: The same latency difference can result in ~180 degree phase difference at the best frequency, due to the small period.
source: The same latency difference, however, can result in ~180 degree phase difference at the best frequency, due to the small period (such as T = 38 µs, where f = 26 kHz).
evidence: This is a calculation demonstrating the relationship between latency and phase at high frequencies.

claim: The latency-induced phase lag of the reticular lamina vibration, compensating for the ~180 degree phase difference observed at low frequencies, accounts for in-phase vibrations of the reticular lamina and basilar membrane at the best frequency.
source: This latency-induced phase lag of the reticular lamina vibration, compensating for the ~180 degree phase difference observed at low frequencies, accounts for in-phase vibrations of the reticular lamina and basilar membrane at the best frequency.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the latency difference results in in-phase vibrations at the best frequency.

claim: The present in vivo results do not conflict with the in vitro observation that both ends of the cylindrical outer hair cells move in opposite directions at low frequencies.
source: Therefore, the present in vivo results do not conflict with the in vitro observation that both ends of the cylindrical outer hair cells move in opposite directions at low frequencies (Brownell et al., 1985; Santos-Sacchi, 1989).
evidence: This is a statement reconciling current findings with prior in vitro observations, supported by citations.

claim: Heterodyne low-coherence interferometry demonstrates in vivo that the outer hair cell-driven reticular lamina vibration occurs after, not before, the basilar membrane vibration.
source: In summary, heterodyne low-coherence interferometry demonstrates in vivo that the outer hair cell-driven reticular lamina vibration occurs after, not before, the basilar membrane vibration.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding of the study.

claim: The reticular lamina and basilar membrane move in opposite directions at low frequencies and in phase near the best frequency.
source: The reticular lamina and basilar membrane move in opposite directions at low frequencies and in phase near the best frequency.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the study.

claim: This experimental finding conflicts with commonly accepted cochlear local feedback theory.
source: This experimental finding conflicts with commonly accepted cochlear local feedback theory and suggests that outer hair cells enhance hearing sensitivity through a global hydromechanical mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings in relation to existing theory.

claim: The experimental findings suggest that outer hair cells enhance hearing sensitivity through a global hydromechanical mechanism.
source: This experimental finding conflicts with commonly accepted cochlear local feedback theory and suggests that outer hair cells enhance hearing sensitivity through a global hydromechanical mechanism.
evidence: This is the main interpretation and conclusion of the study.

claim: Twenty-three young healthy Mongolian gerbils of both sexes at age of 4 to 8 weeks (40–80 g) were used in this study.
source: Twenty-three young healthy Mongolian gerbils of both sexes at age of 4 to 8 weeks (40–80 g) were used in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: A scanning low-coherence heterodyne interferometer was built based on a scanning laser heterodyne interferometer by replacing the helium-neon laser with a modified superluminescent diode with related optical and electronic components.
source: A scanning low-coherence heterodyne interferometer was built based on a scanning laser heterodyne interferometer (Ren, 2002; Ren, 2004; Ren et al., 2011) by replacing the helium-neon laser with a modified superluminescent diode with related optical and electronic components (Ren et al., 2016a; Ren et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus, supported by citations.

claim: The low-coherence interferometer can measure vibrations with a high axial resolution because of the small coherence length.
source: Because of the small coherence length, the low-coherence interferometer can measure vibrations with a high axial resolution (Chen et al., 2011; Hong and Freeman, 2006; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the technique, supported by citations.

claim: The use of low-coherence light and an objective lens with numerical aperture 0.42 provides adequate spatial selectivity for measuring the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibrations in the living cochlea.
source: The use of low-coherence light and an objective lens with numerical aperture 0.42 provides adequate spatial selectivity for measuring the reticular lamina and basilar membrane vibrations in the living cochlea.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical capabilities of the experimental setup.

claim: The interferometer has unprecedented sensitivity, a broad dynamic range, high temporal resolution, and low phase noise, due to the use of a 40-MHz carrier for heterodyne detection.
source: In addition to its unprecedented sensitivity, this interferometer has a broad dynamic range, high temporal resolution, and low phase noise, due to the use of a 40-MHz carrier for heterodyne detection.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical advantages of the experimental apparatus.

claim: A heterodyne interferometer can detect vibration directions without 180-degree phase uncertainty, in contrast to homodyne interferometers.
source: In contrast to homodyne interferometers, a heterodyne interferometer can detect vibration directions without 180-degree phase uncertainty (Hong and Freeman, 2006; Khanna et al., 1986; Lukashkin et al., 2005), which ensured the reliability of the phase measurements in this study.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical advantages of heterodyne interferometry, supported by citations.

claim: The transverse locations of the basilar membrane and reticular lamina were determined by measuring the backscattered light (carrier) level as a function of the transverse location.
source: The transverse locations of the basilar membrane and reticular lamina were determined by measuring the backscattered light (carrier) level as a function of the transverse location.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: The locations of the basilar membrane and reticular lamina were indicated by the two peaks of the backscattered light level and confirmed by the distinct magnitude and phase of the cochlear partition vibrations at the two locations.
source: The locations of the basilar membrane and reticular lamina were indicated by the two peaks of the backscattered light level (Figure 6B) and confirmed by the distinct magnitude and phase of the cochlear partition vibrations at the two locations (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology with reference to data shown in Figure 6.

claim: A cochlea with <5 dB DPOAE decrease was considered sensitive.
source: A cochlea with <5 dB DPOAE decrease was considered sensitive.
evidence: This is a description of the criterion for cochlear sensitivity.

claim: Postmortem data were collected 10 to 30 min after the animal's death from anesthetic overdose.
source: Postmortem data were collected 10 to 30 min after the animal's death from anesthetic overdose.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol for postmortem measurements.
